newsitem.title: USA: Albright, Primakov tackle key issues ahead of summit.
newsitem.headline: Albright, Primakov tackle key issues ahead of summit.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright held talks here on Saturday aimed at making progress on key issues ahead of next week's Helsinki summit.
Primakov, on arrival at Andrews Air Force Base outside the U.S. capital, was met by Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, the Clinton adminstration's pointman on Russia and NATO expansion plans.
He then made an unscheduled stop at the Russian Embassy that delayed his meeting with Albright for an hour. Both planned several hours of discussions.

The two sides are aiming to narrow the gaps on NATO enlargement and on arms control, specifically Russia's failure to ratify the START II strategic arms reduction treaty and U.S. plans to deploy defences against ballistic missiles.
The Americans believe the Russians want the Helsinki summit next Wednesday and Thursday to be a success but have been cautious about predicting a favourable outcome.

It will be the first summit in nearly one year between Clinton and Yeltsin, who until recently was in failing health with heart problems and pneumonia. Some experts say it is one of the most important summits of the post-Cold War era.
Yeltsin and his government have been oppposed to NATO's plans to issue invitations at a July summit in Madrid for former communist states to join the alliance as its first post-Cold War members.
The Russian foreign ministry said Primakov had proposals to make in the row with NATO over its plans to offer membership to Moscow's former communist allies in eastern and central Europe.

Since January Moscow has been negotiating with NATO on a proposed charter defining Russia's ties with the alliance into the 21st century. Officials say Russia's aim is to squeeze as many concessions from Washington and NATO as possible before acceding to inevitable alliance expansion.
The Primakov-Albright talks occur against a background of another NATO concession.

In a move clearly aimed at meeting Russian concerns ahead of next week U.S.-Russia summit in Helsinki, the alliance Friday announced its agreement not to station any permanent new troops in Europe for the foreseeable future.
In a brief statement, issued after a meeting of NATO's 16 ambassadors on Friday, the alliance said it could currently carry out its mission of defending the West by other means.

NATO's latest offer adds to a package of "sweeteners" being assembled to overcome Russia's objections to NATO's near-certain enlargement into Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic later this year and strike a charter with Moscow.
NATO's goal is to complete the charter before the Madrid summit, setting the stage for the alliance to expand while simultaneously building a broad new relationship with Moscow.
In the runup to Helsinki, much focus has been on whether Yeltsin will signal officially at Helsinki his intent to sign a charter by the Madrid meeting.
The charter is seen as a crucial mechanism tying Russia to European security decisions into the next century and calming Moscow's fears about an enlarged NATO someday turning hostile.
But the arms control issues are a critical subtext because they affect Russia's perception of its security.

U.S. officials have said expert-level discussions in Moscow last week produced no movement either on the START II strategic arms reduction treaty and proposed follow-on START III reductions or on ballistic missile defences.
